chunks: Muhammad ibn Ya'qub from Muhammad ibn Yahya from Ahmad ibn Muhammad from Uthman ibn Isa from Sama'ah ibn Mihran said:

I asked him about a man who ate or drank after the dawn had broken had risen in the month of Ramadan. He (peace be upon him) said: If he got up and looked, and did not see the dawn, then ate, and then looked again and saw the dawn, let him complete his fast and there is no re-performance (making up another day) upon him. And if he got up, ate and drank, then looked to the dawn and saw that it had risen, let him complete his fast and make up one other day, because he began with eating before looking, so re-performance is upon him.

key_terms.إِعَادَةَ: Re-performance / making up an additional day
key_terms.طَلَعَ الْفَجْرُ: The rising of the dawn (true dawn/Fajr)

ai.seo_question: What is the ruling if a person eats breakfast after Fajr has actually risen but before they noticed it?
ai.summary: This ruling from al-Isfahani distinguishes between negligence and diligence by prioritizing the act of verification (istibra) over the mere passage of time, a key principle in Shia fiqh. It highlights the scholarly consensus that failing to check for dawn before breaking the fast constitutes a minor fault requiring qada (make-up), whereas checking first validates the fast without penalty. This distinction underscores the importance of proactive caution (ihtiyat) in ritual observance.
